answer: HYPOTHESIS: Increasing government education expenditure has a more favorable (positive) effect on per capita GDP (proxied by GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$) in developing countries (Lower Middle Income, LMC) than in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF). Over 1975–2015, LMC per-capita GDP nearly doubled (≈881→1965) while education expenditure (% of GNI) rose and then declined; a first-difference regression that controls for the common time trend shows a positive but very weak association between changes in education spending and GNI-per-capita growth (slope ≈ +11, R²≈0.01). By contrast, in Sub-Saharan Africa — where GNI per capita is available only for 2011–2015 — education expenditure fell (3.65%→3.15%) while per-capita GDP rose (1555→1634), giving a negative first-difference association (slope ≈ −80, R²≈0.21). Data-grounded hypothesis: the positive effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is weaker or absent in Sub-Saharan Africa relative to developing countries (LMC). This comparison must be interpreted with caution because the Sub-Saharan Africa estimate rests on only 5 years of per-capita-GDP data and cannot be generalized to the full period.

payload.hypothesis: Increasing government education expenditure has a more favorable (positive) effect on per capita GDP (proxied by GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$) in developing countries (LMC) than in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF); the effect is weak/positive in LMC over 1975-2015 and negative/absent in SSF over 2011-2015, with the SSF estimate constrained to only 5 years of per-capita-GDP data.
payload.workflow: 1) Reshape wide CSV (2 groups x 6 WDI series, 1975-2015) to long. 2) Per group (LMC, SSF): descriptive trends of education expenditure (NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS) and GNI per capita (NY.GNP.PCAP.KD); raw correlation; OLS in levels and in first difference (trend-control). 3) Compare first-difference slopes across groups. 4) Write data-grounded hypothesis. LMC used as 'developing countries'; GNI per capita (2015 US$) as per-capita-GDP proxy.
